assessmentSummary.identity: Glute Bridge March is an elevated bilateral floor bridge with an ordered alternating foot-lift-and-replacement sequence while the pelvis remains elevated, followed by a controlled bilateral return.
currentCardFindings: Source 65 has useful coaching notes but lacks an exact canonical cycle, fatigue contract, controlled alternates, calibration, and candidate review gates.
Alternating elevated support is distinct from the bilateral bridge, hip thrust, walkout, single-leg dynamic bridge, and static bridge hold.

proposedTaxonomy.intent: low-load elevated bridge with alternating foot lifts

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Candidate-only exact alternating elevated Bridge March. Treat declared lift height, foot position, range, cadence, pause, cycle count, and rest as modifiers; separately assess hip thrust, walkout, single-leg repetitions, static hold, load, and testing.

currentCardSnapshot.description: From a supine bilateral floor bridge, raise the hips through a comfortable active range. While the pelvis stays elevated, lift and replace one foot under control, then alternate sides. Finish by returning both feet to the floor and lowering under control. One cycle is one left and one right foot lift and replacement within the same elevated bridge. This excludes bilateral bridge repetitions, Hip Thrust, walkout, single-leg bridge repetitions, static hold, testing, forced range, and any undeclared load.

environment.space: room to lie, bridge, alternate foot lifts, and exit safely
environment.changeRule: Changing upper-body support, foot-lift sequence, laterality, load, range, foot position, pause, tempo, dose, surface, or intent requires revalidation.

selectionPrerequisites: can use the supine floor base and exit safely
can hold a small bilateral bridge and replace each foot without symptom escalation or persistent pelvis loss
session logistics and downstream demands fit
excludeOrEscalate: symptom, restriction, unsafe supine base, surface, or communication conflict
sharp, increasing, unfamiliar, neurologic, circulation, breathing, chest, balance, or communication concern
notEstablishedByEvidence: universal foot position, lift height, hip height, dose, recovery, outcome, readiness threshold, or clinical clearance

evidence.sourceTitle: Supine Bridge Exercise: A Narrative Review of the Literature (Part I)
claims: Glute Bridge March begins in an elevated bilateral floor bridge and alternates one controlled foot lift and replacement while the pelvis stays elevated, then ends with a controlled bilateral return.
This excludes a bilateral rise-and-return bridge, hip thrust, walkout, single-leg repetitions, static hold, testing, and forced range.

evidence.sourceTitle: Building a Better Gluteal Bridge: Electromyographic Analysis of Hip Muscle Activity During Modified Single-Leg Bridges
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Alternating foot lift changes the support count and ordered action while the bridge remains elevated.
Support, alternating sequence, range, pause, cadence, external load, and total side count must be declared rather than inferred.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of Modified Bridge Exercise on Trunk Muscle Activity in Healthy Adults: A Cross Sectional Study
claims: Record hip extension, hip flexion, foot support, pelvis, trunk, hip, knee, and spine roles as task mechanics, not isolated-muscle or clinical claims.
No universal activation ranking, foot position, pelvis height, or therapeutic outcome is established.

evidence.sourceTitle: Supine Bridge Exercise: A Narrative Review of the Literature (Part I)
claims: A valid candidate cycle retains an elevated bridge while one foot lifts and returns under control before the other side.
Lumbar extension, pelvis drop, or rotation does not create extra valid range.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Difficulty scores describe exercise complexity and physical demand only, never participant skill, proficiency, age, or classification.
The elevated alternating-support task has more coordination and pelvic-control demand than the bilateral rise-return baseline; independent calibration remains required.

evidence.sourceTitle: A Functional MRI Exploration of Hamstring Activation During the Supine Bridge Exercise
claims: Repeated reduced-support bridge work can change posterior-chain exposure; dose and surrounding work determine fatigue and recovery.
Track left/right lifts, bridge range, tempo, compensation, cramp, symptoms, and same-session hip-extension work.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Use a clear stable floor or mat, space to lie and exit, optional padding, and a clear stop signal.
Readiness and session fit are workout inputs, not participant labels on this exercise card.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Impact of Testing-Parameter Variability on Force Production in the Isometric Single-Leg Long-Lever Bridge: Implications for Training and Testing Rigor in Sporting Environments
evidence.sourcePublisher: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Bridge task interpretation depends on explicit setup and dose; this candidate has no universal volume, range, or recovery claim.
Stop before pain, persistent cramp, pelvis/trunk compensation, breath-holding, or loss of controlled foot replacement.
Instructions must name the floor base, bilateral bridge, small alternating foot lift, quiet pelvis/trunk, controlled replacement, and bilateral exit.
Reduce lift height, bridge range, cycle count, or select another reviewed task before forcing control.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Instruction, stable surface, communication, and progressive exposure are safeguards.
Stop for pain, new symptoms, dizziness, persistent cramp, unsafe surface, or uncorrectable pelvic/trunk loss.

evidence.sourceTitle: A Functional MRI Exploration of Hamstring Activation During the Supine Bridge Exercise
claims: Use Glute Bridge March only when the exact alternating elevated-support task fits the session and fatigue budget; it guarantees no transfer or outcome.
Any change to support, foot lift sequence, load, range, pause, cadence, dose, or substitution reruns selection, logistics, duration, fatigue, and validation.
Athlete support should show the base, quiet pelvis, small lift, controlled replacement, bilateral return, self-check, and stop prompt.
Captions, transcript, stills, audio description, exact media match, and demonstration quality remain human-review requirements.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of Modified Bridge Exercise on Trunk Muscle Activity in Healthy Adults: A Cross Sectional Study
claims: Observe exact base, side sequence, foot pressure, pelvis/trunk organisation, range, cadence, cramp, and first quality loss.
Do not diagnose inhibition or make a different bridge task an automatic substitute.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Candidate supports include padding, reduced range, lower lift, fewer cycles, longer rest, still cues, and another reviewed task when supine work is inaccessible.
Supports do not establish individual readiness or media accessibility.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Ankle Position While Performing One- and Two-Leg Floor Bridging Exercises on Core and Lower Extremity Muscle Recruitment
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Alternating march, walkout, single-leg repetition, static hold, hip thrust, and test endpoints change ordered action, support, contraction, or geometry and require separate assessment.
Foot placement, lift height, cadence, short pause, cycle count, and rest are declared delivery modifiers only under the same alternating elevated-bridge contract.
Three inherited direct YouTube URLs are retained only as unverified candidates; no playback, exact-match, accessibility, quality, reviewer, or approval claim is made.
Privacy-enhanced URLs are review artifacts only and remain non-embeddable until human verification.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge March with Brief Pause
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared short pause changes cadence only when the elevated alternating foot-lift sequence remains intact.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge
alternateAssessments.rationale: Bilateral rise and return has no alternating elevated foot-lift sequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Hip Thrust March
alternateAssessments.rationale: Upper-back support changes geometry, setup, range, and failure conditions.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge Walkout
alternateAssessments.rationale: Heel travel changes knee angle, lever length, and repetition boundary.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
alternateAssessments.rationale: A repeated unilateral rise-return changes the action and side-dose boundary.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge Iso Hold
alternateAssessments.rationale: A static bilateral hold has a different contraction and dose boundary.

alternateAssessments.name: Loaded Glute Bridge March
alternateAssessments.rationale: Declared pelvic load changes physical demand and set-down while preserving the exact elevated alternating-march action.
